newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia guerrillas storm back into cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: Colombia guerrillas storm back into cyberspace.

text.p: Latin America's largest leftist guerrilla army stormed back into cyberspace on Wednesday, reversing the setback it suffered when the plug was pulled on its internet home page last year.
Four months after its high-tech defeat, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) relaunched its magazine Resistencia at http://www.geocities.com/capitolhill/8006.

"In an effort to silence the people and its organisations, the Colombian state, using the terrorist methods that characterise it, closed our home page (in September). But we now have a new temporary site and are fighting to tell people across the world what is really happening in Colombia," international spokesman Marco Leon Calarca told Reuters.
The Mexico City-based rebel group said the original web provider removed the FARC home page after pressure from Colombian government officials and anonymous phone threats.

With its latest victory, the FARC, Latin America's oldest revolutionary movement, regained a toehold on the cyber battlefront alongside Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), whose fighters are holed up in the Japanese Embassy residence in Lima, and Mexico's Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN), both of whom have internet pages.

But it may have a fight on its hands with the new home page provider, whose company rules state it will ban any group that "gives instructional information on illegal activities or promotes harm or injury against any group or individual".

The FARC, which independent political analysts say numbers about 18,000 fighters, was formed as a pro-Soviet force in 1964. Military experts predict the simmering guerrilla uprising on the ground will reach boiling point in 1997.
